questions.question: In the Rabbit of Inaba episode, what does Ōkuninushi do that his eighty elder brothers did not?
options: A. He carries the rabbit to the nearest temple for healing
B. He bathes the rabbit's wounds in fresh water and has it roll in cattail pollen to heal it
C. He challenges the crocodile that skinned the rabbit to a contest
D. He reports the rabbit's suffering to Amaterasu in Takamagahara
questions.explanation: Ōkuninushi instructs the rabbit to bathe in fresh water and roll in cattail pollen — a treatment for the skinned, salt-irritated wounds. His brothers had ignored or mocked the rabbit. This act of practical compassion establishes Ōkuninushi's character as someone who notices suffering and acts.

questions.question: What is 'kuniizukuri' (建国) as Ōkuninushi practices it in the Kojiki?
options: A. A military campaign to conquer the eighty elder brothers
B. The ritual worship of Amaterasu performed in the earthly realm
C. The building of the land — establishing agriculture, medicine, and other civilizational goods
D. The construction of the Izumo Taisha shrine as a condition of the land cession
questions.explanation: Kuniizukuri ('building of the land') refers to Ōkuninushi's culture-hero work: developing the earthly realm through agriculture, medicine, sake brewing, and other practical knowledge, alongside his companion Sukunabikona. He is a builder, not a conqueror — which makes his subsequent dignified abdication coherent with his character.

questions.question: Why do scholars interpret the kuni-yuzuri (land cession) as a political charter rather than (or in addition to) a straightforward myth?
questions.sample_answer: The Izumo region was a real, historically powerful area of Japan with its own religious traditions and patron deity. The kuni-yuzuri encodes the Yamato court's claim to have legitimate authority over this region — not because they conquered it, but because the land's own greatest ruler saw the cosmological order clearly and consented. At the same time, Ōkuninushi's condition — a grand shrine at Izumo — maps onto the real-world Izumo Taisha, one of Japan's most important shrines. The myth explains and legitimizes the ongoing religious and political arrangement between Yamato and Izumo.

questions.question: Ōkuninushi is a descendant of Amaterasu, making his earthly rule part of the heavenly line's original plan.
questions.explanation: Ōkuninushi is from the Susanoo lineage, not the Amaterasu lineage. This is precisely why the kuni-yuzuri is necessary: the earthly realm is ruled by a deity from the earthly/expelled line (Susanoo's), and the heavenly line (Amaterasu's) must reclaim it for Ninigi's descent. The two lineages — heavenly and earthly — are distinct in the Kojiki.

questions.question: What does Ōkuninushi request as the condition of his cession of the earthly realm?
options: A. That his son Kotoshironushi be allowed to rule a portion of the land
B. That a great shrine be built for him at Izumo, as grand as the heavenly palace
C. That he be allowed to accompany Ninigi to Takachiho as a counselor
D. That Amaterasu personally descend to thank him for his contribution to the land
questions.explanation: Ōkuninushi's single condition is a great shrine at Izumo — a palace as grand as the palace of the heavenly gods — where his descendants can maintain divine rites. This becomes the Izumo Taisha (Izumo Grand Shrine), one of Japan's most important and oldest Shinto sites.
